kernels.definition: Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

definitionAnchor.quote: the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price

facts.text: Demand is elastic when the absolute value of the elasticity is greater than one.

anchor.quote: Demand is described as elastic when the absolute value of the elasticity is greater than one

facts.text: Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes.

anchor.quote: Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes

facts.text: The availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity.

anchor.quote: The availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity

kernels.definition: A demand curve shows the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price, holding other factors constant.

definitionAnchor.quote: the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price, holding all other factors constant

facts.text: Demand curves typically slope downward, reflecting the law of demand.

anchor.quote: Demand curves typically slope downward, reflecting the law of demand

facts.text: A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve, while a change in income or tastes shifts the curve.

anchor.quote: A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve

kernels.definition: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers.

definitionAnchor.quote: the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers

facts.text: At the equilibrium price the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and the price has no tendency to change.

anchor.quote: the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change

facts.text: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus that pushes it down; a price below creates a shortage that pushes it up.

anchor.quote: a surplus pushes it down, and when the price is below equilibrium a shortage pushes it up

kernels.definition: A wage-price spiral is a self-reinforcing cycle in which rising prices lead workers to demand higher wages, and higher wage costs lead firms to raise prices further.

definitionAnchor.quote: rising prices lead workers to demand higher wages, and the higher wage costs lead firms to raise prices further

facts.text: The wage-price spiral is positive feedback: an initial change is amplified rather than damped.

anchor.quote: positive feedback, in which an initial change is amplified rather than damped

facts.text: Unlike negative feedback, positive feedback drives the system further from where it started.

anchor.quote: positive feedback drives the system further from where it started

kernels.definition: Consumer choice theory models how a consumer maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint.

definitionAnchor.quote: how a consumer maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint

facts.text: The consumer selects the affordable bundle of goods that yields the highest satisfaction.

anchor.quote: selects the affordable bundle of goods that yields the highest satisfaction

facts.text: At the optimal choice, utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget, so the consumer faces a tradeoff between goods.

anchor.quote: utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget, so the consumer faces a tradeoff between goods

kernels.definition: An economic model is a simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest.

definitionAnchor.quote: a simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest

facts.text: Models such as supply and demand make assumptions, like rational choice or perfect competition, that do not hold exactly.

anchor.quote: make assumptions, like rational choice or perfect competition, that do not hold exactly

facts.text: A model is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand, and misleading when a key assumption breaks.

mcItems.q: Which expression gives price elasticity of demand?
op: percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
change in quantity demanded divided by change in price
percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
change in price divided by change in quantity demanded
mcItems.ex: This is correct because elasticity compares the percentage change in quantity demanded with the percentage change in price. The slope-style option is a common misconception because it uses raw changes instead of percentages.

mcItems.q: Which feature most strongly makes demand more elastic for a good?
op: having many close substitutes
being a necessity for buyers
having no change in price
selling at a high total quantity
mcItems.ex: This is correct because the availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity. The necessity option is the tempting misconception, but necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes.

keyTerms.df: A ratio showing how quantity demanded responds to a price change.
keyTerms.eg: If a price rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 20%, the elasticity is -2.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same as the market price level.
keyTerms.cx: It measures responsiveness, not the price itself.

keyTerms.df: Demand that changes proportionally more than the price does.
keyTerms.eg: A small fare increase that leads many riders to switch to another route shows elastic demand when close alternatives are available.
keyTerms.mi: Any good with a high price is elastic.
keyTerms.cx: Elasticity depends on how buyers respond and on substitutes, not on the price tag alone.

mcItems.q: A coffee shop raises the price of its iced latte, and customers buy fewer lattes. Which description fits this evidence best?
op: The quantity demanded moves along the demand curve.
The demand curve shifts right because price rose.
The demand curve shifts left because price rose.
The good becomes more elastic because price rose.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is the movement along the demand curve: a price change leads to movement, not a shift. The other choices confuse price changes with shifts, or mix up elasticity with the way the curve itself changes.

mcItems.q: A designer jacket becomes fashionable, so buyers are willing to purchase more at every price. What happens?
op: The demand curve shifts right.
The quantity demanded moves down the curve.
The curve becomes flatter because tastes changed.
The price level falls because demand changed.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is that the demand curve shifts right: a change in tastes shifts the curve. The other choices either describe a movement caused by price, treat slope as the same thing as a shift, or infer a price result that is not given by the claim.

keyTerms.df: A relationship showing how much of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, with other influences held fixed.
keyTerms.eg: When the price of a movie ticket changes, the demand curve is used to trace how much ticket quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at that price.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same thing as a full market outcome after buyers and sellers bargain.
keyTerms.cx: The curve summarizes buyer willingness and ability at different prices; it is not the final traded outcome.

keyTerms.df: A change in the quantity demanded caused by a change in the good’s own price.
keyTerms.eg: If the price of lemonade rises and customers buy fewer cups, the point slides to a different spot on the same demand curve.
keyTerms.mi: Any change in buyer purchases must mean the entire curve shifted.
keyTerms.cx: A price change moves you along one curve; shifts come from other influences such as income or tastes.

mcItems.q: A store lists a good at a price that is above the market level where buyers and sellers agree. What is the most likely market result?
op: A surplus forms, which puts downward pressure on the price.
A shortage forms, which puts upward pressure on the price.
The market is in equilibrium, so the price has no tendency to change.
Demand shifts right, so the price must rise because buyers prefer it.
mcItems.ex: A surplus forms, which puts downward pressure on the price. The other choices confuse equilibrium with fairness, shortage, or a demand shift; only a price above the balance point creates excess supply under the given claims.

mcItems.q: At one price, buyers want exactly the same amount that sellers offer. What does this tell you about the market price?
op: It is the equilibrium price, so there is no tendency for it to change.
It is above equilibrium, so a surplus must be present.
It is below equilibrium, so a shortage must be present.
It is the highest price buyers will accept, so demand has ended.
mcItems.ex: It is the equilibrium price, so there is no tendency for it to change. The common mistake is to treat equilibrium as a fairness judgment or a ceiling; here, equal quantities from buyers and sellers identify the balance point instead.

keyTerms.df: The level where the two sides of the market match in quantity.
keyTerms.eg: In a class simulation, the trading price settled where the number of units students wanted to buy matched the number offered for sale.
keyTerms.mi: It is the price that feels fair to most people.
keyTerms.cx: The matching quantities matter, not a judgment about fairness.

keyTerms.df: An excess supply situation that appears when sellers offer more than buyers want at a given price.
keyTerms.eg: When a café set its sandwich price too high, several sandwiches remained unsold at the end of lunch.
keyTerms.mi: It means the good is in short supply and people cannot find enough of it.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that excess supply pushes the price downward, not upward.

mcItems.q: Which statement best matches a wage-price spiral?
op: Higher prices can lead workers to seek higher wages, and those higher labor costs can push more
Prices move because of a one-time shortage, then the change stops on its own
Wage changes and price changes cancel each other out, so the system returns to its start
Firms raise prices only when demand shifts outward, not when wages rise
mcItems.ex: The first option matches a cycle in which rising prices lead to higher wage demands, and higher wages then lead firms to raise prices again. A common misconception is to treat the process as a one-time change or a simple demand shift, but the claim describes a reinforcing loop, not a single step.

mcItems.q: In this course, what does positive feedback mean for a wage-price spiral?
op: An initial rise is amplified, so the system moves farther from its starting point
A price increase is offset, so the system automatically returns to the same level
Only workers react, while firms do not change prices afterward
The effect is fixed at the first change, so later responses do not matter
mcItems.ex: The first option is correct because positive feedback amplifies the initial change rather than damping it. The most plausible mistake is to confuse it with negative feedback, which would push the system back toward where it started.

keyTerms.df: A loop where rising prices can trigger higher wage demands, and those higher wages can then push prices up again.

keyTerms.mi: It is just any situation where wages go up once and prices happen to rise later.

keyTerms.df: A process in which the initial change is strengthened instead of reduced.

mcItems.q: A student is deciding whether a market diagram helps answer a question about food prices. Which choice best describes when an economic model is useful?
op: It keeps only the features relevant to the question and leaves out the rest.
It is useful only when every assumption is exactly true.
It is useful only when the market is perfectly fair.
It must include every detail so the result is complete.
mcItems.ex: It is useful when it simplifies reality by keeping the features that matter for the question. A common misconception is that a model works only if every assumption is literally exact, but a model can still be useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand.

mcItems.q: A supply-and-demand model is used to estimate the effect of a tax, but one key assumption does not fit the market. What is the best conclusion?
op: The model may be misleading because a key assumption breaks.
The model is always wrong because all assumptions are false.
The model proves the tax is unfair.
The model must predict the exact price with no error.
mcItems.ex: The model may be misleading because a key assumption breaks. A common mistake is to treat any imperfect assumption as fatal, but the claim is narrower: models are useful when assumptions are close enough and misleading when a key assumption fails.

keyTerms.df: A simplified representation that keeps what matters for a question and leaves out the rest.
keyTerms.eg: In class, a demand-and-supply diagram can serve as an economic model for studying how a price change affects quantity traded.
keyTerms.mi: It is a complete copy of the real economy.
keyTerms.cx: The model is not a full replica; it is a focused tool that omits details irrelevant to the question.

mcItems.q: Which description best matches a wage-price spiral?
op: Prices rise, workers ask for higher wages, and firms then raise prices again.
Prices rise and then immediately return to their original level.
Wages rise only because workers become more productive.
Prices fall because higher wages always reduce demand.
mcItems.ex: It is a self-reinforcing cycle where price increases trigger higher wage demands and more price increases. It is not a return to the starting point.

Negative feedback that dampens the initial change.
No feedback because wages and prices move independently.
A one-time shock with no further effects.
mcItems.ex: Positive feedback makes the first change grow rather than shrink. It is not negative feedback that pushes the system back.

mcItems.q: Which statement best describes consumer choice theory?
op: It shows how a consumer maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint.
It says consumers always buy the cheapest bundle available.
It assumes satisfaction is highest when spending exceeds the budget.
It predicts people choose randomly when prices change.
mcItems.ex: It matches maximizing utility within a budget. The mistake is thinking the cheapest bundle is always best.

mcItems.q: What is true at the consumer's optimal choice?
op: Utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget.
The consumer can still raise utility by buying more of every good.
The consumer has no tradeoff between goods.
The budget no longer matters once the best bundle is found.
mcItems.ex: At the best bundle, more utility would require breaking the budget. The trap is saying the budget stops mattering.

mcItems.q: Which expression gives price elasticity of demand?
op: percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
change in quantity demanded divided by change in price
percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
change in price divided by change in quantity demanded
mcItems.ex: This is correct because elasticity compares the percentage change in quantity demanded with the percentage change in price. The slope-style option is a common misconception because it uses raw changes instead of percentages.

mcItems.q: Which feature most strongly makes demand more elastic for a good?
op: having many close substitutes
being a necessity for buyers
having no change in price
selling at a high total quantity
mcItems.ex: This is correct because the availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity. The necessity option is the tempting misconception, but necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes.

keyTerms.df: A ratio showing how quantity demanded responds to a price change.
keyTerms.eg: If a price rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 20%, the elasticity is -2.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same as the market price level.
keyTerms.cx: It measures responsiveness, not the price itself.

keyTerms.df: Demand that changes proportionally more than the price does.
keyTerms.eg: A small fare increase that leads many riders to switch to another route shows elastic demand when close alternatives are available.
keyTerms.mi: Any good with a high price is elastic.
keyTerms.cx: Elasticity depends on how buyers respond and on substitutes, not on the price tag alone.

mcItems.q: A coffee shop raises the price of its iced latte, and customers buy fewer lattes. Which description fits this evidence best?
op: The quantity demanded moves along the demand curve.
The demand curve shifts right because price rose.
The demand curve shifts left because price rose.
The good becomes more elastic because price rose.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is the movement along the demand curve: a price change leads to movement, not a shift. The other choices confuse price changes with shifts, or mix up elasticity with the way the curve itself changes.

mcItems.q: A designer jacket becomes fashionable, so buyers are willing to purchase more at every price. What happens?
op: The demand curve shifts right.
The quantity demanded moves down the curve.
The curve becomes flatter because tastes changed.
The price level falls because demand changed.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is that the demand curve shifts right: a change in tastes shifts the curve. The other choices either describe a movement caused by price, treat slope as the same thing as a shift, or infer a price result that is not given by the claim.

keyTerms.df: A relationship showing how much of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, with other influences held fixed.
keyTerms.eg: When the price of a movie ticket changes, the demand curve is used to trace how much ticket quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at that price.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same thing as a full market outcome after buyers and sellers bargain.
keyTerms.cx: The curve summarizes buyer willingness and ability at different prices; it is not the final traded outcome.

keyTerms.df: A change in the quantity demanded caused by a change in the good’s own price.
keyTerms.eg: If the price of lemonade rises and customers buy fewer cups, the point slides to a different spot on the same demand curve.
keyTerms.mi: Any change in buyer purchases must mean the entire curve shifted.
keyTerms.cx: A price change moves you along one curve; shifts come from other influences such as income or tastes.

mcItems.q: A store lists a good at a price that is above the market level where buyers and sellers agree. What is the most likely market result?
op: A surplus forms, which puts downward pressure on the price.
A shortage forms, which puts upward pressure on the price.
The market is in equilibrium, so the price has no tendency to change.
Demand shifts right, so the price must rise because buyers prefer it.
mcItems.ex: A surplus forms, which puts downward pressure on the price. The other choices confuse equilibrium with fairness, shortage, or a demand shift; only a price above the balance point creates excess supply under the given claims.

mcItems.q: At one price, buyers want exactly the same amount that sellers offer. What does this tell you about the market price?
op: It is the equilibrium price, so there is no tendency for it to change.
It is above equilibrium, so a surplus must be present.
It is below equilibrium, so a shortage must be present.
It is the highest price buyers will accept, so demand has ended.
mcItems.ex: It is the equilibrium price, so there is no tendency for it to change. The common mistake is to treat equilibrium as a fairness judgment or a ceiling; here, equal quantities from buyers and sellers identify the balance point instead.

keyTerms.df: The level where the two sides of the market match in quantity.
keyTerms.eg: In a class simulation, the trading price settled where the number of units students wanted to buy matched the number offered for sale.
keyTerms.mi: It is the price that feels fair to most people.
keyTerms.cx: The matching quantities matter, not a judgment about fairness.

keyTerms.df: An excess supply situation that appears when sellers offer more than buyers want at a given price.
keyTerms.eg: When a café set its sandwich price too high, several sandwiches remained unsold at the end of lunch.
keyTerms.mi: It means the good is in short supply and people cannot find enough of it.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that excess supply pushes the price downward, not upward.

keyTerms.df: A loop where rising prices can trigger higher wage demands, and those higher wages can then push prices up again.
keyTerms.eg: In a lesson on inflation feedback, students trace how higher prices can lead to higher wages and then to another round of price increases.
keyTerms.mi: It is just any situation where wages go up once and prices happen to rise later.
keyTerms.cx: That correction matters because the term refers to a self-reinforcing cycle, not merely two separate events.

keyTerms.df: A process in which the initial change is strengthened instead of reduced.
keyTerms.eg: When the class models the spiral, a first price increase can be followed by further increases rather than being damped away.
keyTerms.mi: It always means the system becomes fairer or more stable.
keyTerms.cx: In this context, the key idea is amplification, not fairness or automatic stability.
